title: Safe Driving Habits
summary: How to avoid distraction, drowsiness and road rage, wear belts and set up your seat correctly, and keep your car safe to drive.

rows: Visual (eyes off the road)
Looking at a phone, a billboard or a crash scene.
Manual (hands off the wheel)
Eating, grooming, unwrapping food or reaching for things.
Cognitive (mind off driving)
Daydreaming, a phone call, a heated argument or thinking hard about a problem.

blocks.text: Texting is the worst because it does all three at once. Reading a message is as distracting as typing one. A 5-second look at a phone at 55 mph means driving about the length of a football field blind.
Mental distractions are as dangerous as looking away. Your eyes can be aimed right at a red light while your mind never notices it.

blocks.caption: Phone laws vary by state, including hand-held bans and rules for new drivers. See your State Cheat Sheet.

items: Let calls go to voicemail. Call back after you park, or have a passenger make the call.
Hands-free calls are still a cognitive distraction that slows your reactions.
Set your GPS and plan your route before you start moving.
If a child needs help, pull over to a safe place first.
Secure pets in a carrier, kennel or pet harness. Never drive with a pet on your lap.
Do not "rubberneck" at crashes or work zones; watch your own lane.
Put off arguments and emotional talks until you are stopped somewhere safe.

blocks.text: Never leave children or pets alone in a parked car, even on a mild day. The inside heats up quickly.
A car that drifts within its lane and changes speed for no reason may have a distracted driver. Give it extra room and take extra care when passing.

Sleep is the only cure for drowsiness. Opening a window or turning up the radio will not keep you awake. You can fall asleep for a few seconds without knowing it, so never push on for "just a few more miles."

items: Warning signs: heavy eyelids, constant yawning, drifting out of your lane and jerking back, and hitting rumble strips.
Higher risk: shift workers driving after work, young drivers, people with sleep disorders, and anyone driving when they would normally be asleep.
Highway hypnosis is a drowsy, trance-like state caused by long, unchanging roads. Keep your eyes moving, check mirrors and gauges, and stop to rest.

blocks.text: Before a long trip, get a good night's sleep, plan regular breaks, and share the driving if you can.

blocks.caption: Everyone, in every seat, on every trip. Seat belt and child seat laws vary; see your State Cheat Sheet.

items: Wear the lap belt snug and low on your hips, and the shoulder belt across your shoulder and chest.
Never put the shoulder belt behind your back or under your arm. A lap belt alone will not keep your head and chest off the dash or wheel.
If your car has an automatic shoulder belt, buckle the separate lap belt too, or you can slide out underneath.
Pregnant? Wear both parts: lap belt low, under the belly; shoulder belt across the chest, beside the belly.
Airbags work with seat belts; they do not replace them.
Being thrown from a car greatly raises your chance of death. A belted person is also more likely to stay conscious and escape a fire or water crash.

rows: Distance from airbag
At least 10 inches from your breastbone to the center of the wheel. Short drivers should sit as far back as they can while still reaching the pedals.
Rear-facing child seat
Never in front of an active airbag.
Children 12 and under
Ride in the back seat, properly restrained. Most crashes are frontal, and airbags can badly hurt children.
Babies
Never held on a lap. Crash forces make it impossible to hold on.

sections.heading: Set up your seat, mirrors and grip

items: Adjust your seat first, since moving it changes what you see in the mirrors.
Set the head restraint directly behind your head, not down at your neck, to help prevent whiplash.
Set the inside mirror to frame the whole rear window from your normal seat.
Set each side mirror so you can just see the side of your car when you lean toward that side.
Put heavy loose items in the trunk or secure them; in a sudden stop or crash they keep moving and can hit you. Clear the driver's floor so nothing rolls under the pedals.

blocks.text: Hold the wheel with both hands on opposite sides. Most handbooks recommend 9 and 3 or 8 and 4 o'clock; a few also accept 10 and 2. Lower positions keep a deploying airbag from throwing your arms into your face.
In push-pull (hand-to-hand) steering, one hand pushes up while the other slides and pulls down. Your hands never cross over each other.
Aggressive driving, such as speeding, tailgating and unsafe lane changes, breaks traffic laws. Road rage goes further, into threats or violence, and breaks criminal laws.

items: If someone cuts you off or gestures, do not take it personally. Avoid eye contact, do not gesture back, and give them room.
If someone tailgates or flashes their lights to pass, let them go. Do not speed up, block them or brake suddenly.
If an angry driver follows you, do not go home and do not get out. Drive to a police station or a busy public place.
Leave early and allow extra time for delays so you do not feel rushed.
If you are very angry, upset or excited, calm down before you drive, or let someone else drive.

rows: Tire pressure
Use the number on the driver's door jamb label or in the owner's manual. Check with a gauge while tires are cold.
Worn tires
Longer stops, harder turns, more hydroplaning and more flats.
Shaking wheel or pulling
Have a mechanic check the tires, wheels and steering.
Wipers and glass
Replace blades that streak. Keep the windshield clean inside and out, since dirt makes glare worse, and keep washer fluid full.
Exhaust
A loud rumble or exhaust smell inside can mean a leak that lets in deadly carbon monoxide. Fix it right away.

items: Do not use cruise control on wet, icy or snowy roads.
Never let the engine run in a garage, even with the garage door open. Carbon monoxide builds up fast. Back the car outside to warm it up.
If you sit in an idling car in snow, keep the tailpipe clear and open a window slightly.

keyPoints: Distractions are visual, manual or cognitive; texting is all three, and hands-free calls still distract your mind.
Set your GPS before you drive, pull over to deal with kids or calls, and secure pets.
Only sleep cures drowsiness; drifting, yawning and heavy eyelids mean stop and rest.
Lap belt low on the hips, shoulder belt across the chest; airbags work with belts, not instead of them.
Sit at least 10 inches from the airbag; children 12 and under ride in back, never in front of an active airbag in a rear-facing seat.
Adjust the seat first, then the head restraint and mirrors; hold the wheel at 9 and 3 or 8 and 4.
Never challenge an aggressive driver; if followed, go to a police station or busy public place.
Check tires cold, fix exhaust leaks right away, and never idle the engine in a garage.
